subject: geography
title: Food Chains and Webs
welcome_lead: Who eats whom? Discover how energy flows through ecosystems via food chains and webs.
meta_desc: KS3 Geography adventure on food chains, food webs and energy flow.
final_note: Great work! You now understand how energy flows in nature.

concepts.def: Plant that makes its own food from sunlight.
Animal that eats plants or other animals.
Breaks down dead material, e.g. fungi.

walkthroughs.body_html: The Sun powers plants (producers). Plants are eaten by herbivores. Herbivores are eaten by carnivores. Energy passes up the chain.
A food chain shows one line of energy. A food web shows many connections — more realistic because animals eat lots of things.
Fungi and bacteria break down dead plants and animals, returning nutrients to the soil.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between qualitative and quantitative data?
options: Rainforest layers exist because trees grow in age order tallest to shortest.
Qualitative data means high-quality data and quantitative means a lot of data.
Quantitative data is always more scientific and reliable than qualitative.
Quantitative data is numerical and measurable (traffic counts, river width); qualitative data is descriptive and non-numerical (interview quotes, photo descriptions, field sketches).

mcqs.q: Why does the tropical rainforest have distinct vertical layers?
options: Qualitative data means high-quality data and quantitative means a lot of data.
Competition for light: emergents (40m+), canopy (capturing most light), understorey (shade-tolerant) and forest floor (sparse vegetation due to low light) — each adapted to its light level.
Rainforest layers exist because trees grow in age order tallest to shortest.
Rainforest layers exist because different animals live at different heights.
Qualitative data means high-quality data and quantitative means a lot of data.
Earthquakes are caused by magma rising up to the surface.
Earthquakes are caused by the Earth's core overheating.
The sudden release of built-up stress along faults at plate boundaries as rocks slip past each other, generating seismic waves.
